summary: Explains how to translate between the older Diversion header field and the standardized History-Info header field in SIP, both used to describe call forwarding. The Diversion header is non-standard but still widely deployed, so systems need a way to interwork.

plainLanguage.summary: When a call is forwarded, the SIP messages can carry a record of where it came from and why it was redirected. There are two header fields for this: the standard History-Info header, and an older Diversion header that was never standardised but is widely deployed. This RFC gives the precise rules for converting one into the other, so a call can cross between networks that use different ones without losing the history.

questions: how to map diversion header to history-info
what is the sip diversion header
subtitle: How to translate between the old Diversion header and the standard History-Info header in SIP.

tldr.problem: Two SIP header fields carry the same information about why a call was forwarded. History-Info is the standard one, but the older Diversion header was implemented by many manufacturers and is still deployed, so the two have to be made to work together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an interworking function, normally a border device that knows it sits between one region using History-Info and one using Diversion. It gives exact rules for converting entries in both directions, including how reasons, counters and privacy settings map.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 6044. It also says plainly that new implementation and deployment of the Diversion header field are strongly discouraged.

today: RFC 7544 was published in August 2015 as an Informational document and obsoletes RFC 6044, the earlier version of the same mapping. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The document itself advises against new implementation and deployment of the Diversion header field.

sections.title: Why Two Header Fields Carry the Same Information
sections.content:
For some services built on VoIP, such as voicemail, interactive voice recognition and automatic call distribution, it helps the called SIP user agent to identify from whom and why the session was diverted. For that information to be used by service providers or applications, it has to pass through the network. Two SIP header fields can carry it: the History-Info header field defined in RFC 7044, and the historic Diversion header field defined in RFC 5806.

Although the Diversion header field is not standardized, it has been widely implemented, so it is useful to have guidelines that make it interwork with the standard History-Info header field. The RFC notes that new implementation and deployment of the Diversion header field are strongly discouraged, and that the document provides a mechanism for translating header field content between the two.

The background is that the obsoleted History-Info header field of RFC 4244, and its extension for forming SIP service URIs, used to be recommended by the IETF to convey redirection information, and were also recommended in the 3GPP Communication Diversion specification. The Diversion header field was originally described in a document submitted to the SIP Working Group and eventually published as an Independent Submission, RFC 5806, for the historical record; it serves as a reference for this RFC. It contains a list of diverting URIs and associated information giving the reason for the call diversion. Most of the first SIP-based implementations implemented it when no standard solution was ready to deploy, and the IETF standardized History-Info partly because it can transport general history information, which lets the receiving party determine how and why the session was received.

The two header fields have different syntaxes. The main difference is that History-Info is written in chronological order, whereas the Diversion header field applies a reverse chronology, so the first diversion entry read corresponds to the last diverting user. Because History-Info may hold more than call diversion information, it is critical to avoid losing information, and the retargeting cause URI parameter described in RFC 4458 is used to carry the call forwarding reason.
sections.plainLanguage: Both headers answer the same question, but they list the answer in opposite directions and they cover different amounts: Diversion records only forwarded calls, while History-Info records every change of destination. A device at the border between the two kinds of network has to translate, and the RFC tells it how.

sections.title: Retargeting and Call Diversion
sections.content:
The RFC gives the vocabulary used throughout. Retarget and redirect refer to the process of a proxy server or user agent client changing a Request-URI in a request, and thus changing the target of the request. This includes changing the Request-URI because of a location service lookup and redirect processing, and it also includes internal changes of the URI within a proxy before the request is forwarded. The term retarget is defined in RFC 7044.

Call forwarding, call diversion and communication diversion are equivalent terms for the Communication Diversion supplementary services, which are based on the ISDN communication diversion supplementary services and defined in the 3GPP specification. They apply to entities intended to modify the original destination of an IP multimedia session during or before the session is established.

The document does not intend to describe when or how the two header fields should be used. The scope of each is what matters for the mapping. The Diversion header field has exactly the same scope as the call diversion service, and each entry reflects one call diversion invocation; it is used for recording call forwarding information that could be useful to network entities downstream, and it is implemented by several manufacturers and deployed in networks. The History-Info header field is used to store all retargeting information, including call diversion information, and conveys call-diversion-related information by using a cause URI parameter in the relevant entry.

The RFC draws a limit. The use of the cause URI parameter for a call diversion is specific to the 3GPP specification. RFC 4458 focuses on retargeting toward a voicemail server and does not say whether the cause parameter should be added for other cases, so implementations that do not use the cause parameter for call forwarding information are not considered for the mapping described here.
sections.plainLanguage: Two words cover most of the document. Retargeting means changing where a request is going. Call diversion means a call being forwarded as a service, with a reason attached. The mapping only works for networks that record the reason the standard way, using a cause parameter on the address.

sections.title: How the Two Header Fields Coexist
sections.content:
Because both header fields address call forwarding needs, diverting information could be mixed up or inconsistent if both were present in an uncoordinated fashion in an INVITE request. Diversion and History-Info header fields must therefore not independently coexist in the same session signalling.

The RFC defines an interworking function. In the normal case, the network topology assumption is that the interworking is performed by a specific SIP border device that is aware, by configuration, that it is at the border between two regions, one using History-Info and one using Diversion. Since History-Info is the standard solution, a network using Diversion must be able to provide information to a network using History-Info, and to avoid coexistence of header fields the Diversion header field is replaced, as often as possible, by the History-Info header field in the INVITE request during the interworking.

Because History-Info has a wider scope than Diversion, it may be used for needs and services other than call diversion, and it acts as a session history that can store all successive Request-URI values. Even though it would be better to remove the History-Info header field after creating the Diversion header field, the History-Info header field must remain unmodified in the SIP signalling if it contains supplementary, non-diversion information. It is possible to have History-Info header fields with values that cannot be mapped into the Diversion header field; in that case no interworking is performed and what to do is left to each implementation, which is out of scope here. The RFC concludes that local policies should minimise the loss of information and find the best way to keep it up to the terminating user agent.

The interworking applies only for INVITE requests. In 3xx responses both header fields could be present, and a proxy that wants to interwork should apply the conversion there. When a recursing proxy redirects an initial INVITE after receiving a 3xx response, it should add as a last entry either a Diversion header field or a History-Info header field, according to its capabilities, in the forwarded INVITE. In SIP responses other than 100, the History-Info header field is not used for the call forwarding service and should not be changed into a Diversion header field, and the destination network must be transparent to a received History-Info header field.
sections.plainLanguage: The two headers must never both be floating around the same call doing different things, so one device at the border converts one into the other. History-Info is the one that survives, because it can hold more than just forwarding history, and it is left untouched if it carries anything the Diversion header cannot express.

sections.title: Privacy and Security at the Boundary
sections.content:
When a SIP message is forwarded to a domain for which the SIP intermediary is not responsible, a Privacy Service at the boundary of the domain applies the appropriate privacy based on the value of the Privacy header field in the message header, or in the privacy parameter within the concerned header. For History-Info, that is the Privacy header field included as the headers component of the hi-targeted-to-uri in the individual entries, with the priv-value history. For Diversion, it is the diversion-privacy parameter privacy in each header field.

If there is a Privacy header field in the message header of a request with a priv-value of header or history, then all the hi-targeted-to-uris in the entries associated with the domain for which the intermediary is responsible are anonymised, by changing any that have not already been anonymised to the anonymous SIP URI anonymous@anonymous.invalid. If the Privacy header field appears in the headers component of a hi-targeted-to-uri with a priv-value of history, then all the concerned entries must be anonymised in the same way before forwarding. The Privacy Service must remove the Privacy header field from the headers component and the priv-value of history from the message header before forwarding, and if no priv-values remain it must remove the Privacy header field from the request.

For the Diversion header field, a Privacy header field in the message header with a priv-value of header means all the addresses in the Diversion header fields are anonymised before forwarding. And for each Diversion header field or each entry in it, a diversion-privacy parameter with a value of full, uri or name means the concerned address must be anonymised, and the diversion-privacy parameter must then be removed from the header. The privacy information interworking described later in the document must only be considered within a trusted domain that ensures correct application of the privacy requirements.

The Security Considerations section adds that the considerations of RFC 7044 and RFC 5806 apply, together with the privacy ones above. Using either header field requires application of the privacy and integrity requested by each diverting user or entity. Without integrity, the requested privacy functions could be downgraded or eliminated, potentially exposing identity information. Without confidentiality, eavesdroppers on the network, or any intermediaries between the user and the Privacy Service, could see the very personal information the user asked to have obscured. Unauthorised insertion, deletion or modification of these header fields can provide misleading information to users and applications, and an entity that can supply a redirection reason should be able to suppress it in accordance with the privacy requirements of the user concerned.
sections.plainLanguage: The headers carry names and numbers, so the boundary device has to honour the privacy requests attached to them, replacing addresses with the anonymous form where asked. The RFC is blunt about the risk: without integrity checks a privacy request can be quietly dropped, and without encryption anyone on the path can read the very details the user asked to hide.

sections.title: Turning Diversion into History-Info
sections.content:
The rules in this section apply only when no History-Info header field is present in the INVITE request; if at least one is present, the interworking function must adapt its behaviour to respect the chronological order.

For N Diversion entries, N+1 History-Info entries must be created. To create them in the same order as during a session establishment, the Diversion entries are mapped from the bottom-most to the top-most. The first History-Info entry contains a hi-targeted-to-uri with the name-addr of the bottom-most Diversion header field, a hi-index set to 1, and, if a privacy parameter is present in that Diversion entry, a Privacy header field escaped in the History-Info header field as the table describes. For each of the remaining Diversion entries, the History-Info entries are created from top to bottom: the name-addr becomes the hi-targeted-to-uri, the reason of the previous Diversion entry becomes a cause URI parameter added in each entry except the first, the counter becomes part of the hi-index, the privacy value becomes an escaped Privacy header field, and an mp-param is added in each created entry except the first, set to the index value of the preceding entry.

A last History-Info entry is created with a hi-targeted-to-uri holding the Request-URI of the INVITE request, a cause parameter taken from the top-most Diversion entry, an index set to the previous index extended with a new level .1, and an mp parameter set to the index of the previous entry.

The RFC adds four notes. For other optional Diversion parameters there is no recommendation, because History-Info has no equivalent parameters. For reasons that map to a default cause value, another value could be chosen; the cause parameter offers fewer possible values than the diversion-reason parameter, but the list was considered sufficient to implement the 3GPP diversion service because it covers a large portion of cases. The Diversion header field can carry a tel URI in the name-addr parameter; History-Info can also hold a tel URI, but if the entry has to be completed with a SIP header field such as Reason or Privacy, or a SIP URI parameter such as cause or target, the tel URI must be converted into a SIP URI, and because a valid host and port is hard to determine the RFC suggests using a SIP URI with user=phone and a domain set to unknown.invalid. Finally, the Diversion counter retains the number of successive redirections and History-Info has no equivalent, because counting in History-Info means counting the cause parameters; the placeholder entry makes it possible for the entries to reflect the real number of diversions.
sections.plainLanguage: Each forwarded call becomes one entry, plus one more for the party the call was actually sent to, and the list is turned round so it reads in the order the calls happened. The reason for each forwarding is translated into the standard set of SIP status codes, and where a call was forwarded several times a placeholder entry records the gap.

sections.title: Turning History-Info into Diversion
sections.content:
In the other direction, the History-Info entries are mapped from the top-most to the bottom-most, and the first entry selected is mapped into the last Diversion entry, and so on. One Diversion entry must be created for each History-Info entry that has a cause parameter with a value listed in RFC 4458.

The RFC defines two kinds of entry to help readers follow the mapping. A Target_entry is a hi-entry containing a cause URI parameter with such a value; it holds the diversion reason and the address of the target of the call forwarding, and per RFC 7044 it may also contain a target parameter set to mp. A Diverting_entry is found for each such entry: if there is an mp header field parameter, the hi-entry whose hi-index matches the value of the mp parameter holds the diverting party address, its possible privacy and, where the retargeting was caused by a received SIP response, the SIP reason; if there is no mp parameter, the same information is found in the hi-entry that precedes the identified entry. Per RFC 7044 all retargeting entries must point to a hi-entry containing an mp parameter, but for backward compatibility it may be absent from some received entries.

The mapping itself takes the hi-targeted-to-uri of the Diverting_entry as the name-addr, the cause parameter of the Target_entry as the reason, setting the counter to 1, and the escaped Privacy header field of the Diverting_entry as the privacy parameter. Again, for other optional History-Info parameters there is no recommendation, because Diversion has no equivalent parameters.

When the History-Info header field is interpreted to create a Diversion header field, some precautions must be taken. If the History-Info header field contains only call forwarding information, it must be deleted after the interworking. If it contains other information, only the information of concern to the diverting user is used to create the Diversion entries, and the History-Info header field must be kept as received and forwarded downstream, because a service may need to know whether a particular application server has yet been invoked in the signalling path, and losing that history on the way through a network that only supports Diversion would be a loss. If a Diversion header field is also present in the incoming INVITE, only the diversion information present in History-Info but not in Diversion is inserted from the last entry into the existing Diversion header field, and the chronological order then cannot be certified. The RFC also handles a forking case, where History-Info entries with an incremented index parameter record sequential forking; those entries could possibly be mapped if they contain a call forwarding cause parameter, and the interworking entity could choose to create only a Diversion entry or not to apply the interworking, according to local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Going the other way, the RFC works out which entries in the history actually describe a forwarded call, finds the party that did the forwarding in the entry before each one, and builds a Diversion header out of those. Anything in the history that is not about forwarding is left in place rather than thrown away, because other services may be relying on it.

cells: Reverse chronology: the first entry read is the last diverting user
All retargeting information, including call diversion
No equivalent; the cause parameter carries it
Privacy header field escaped in the hi-targeted-to-uri
The rc, mp and np header field parameters
